mainTopic: Why the משנה lists each fined case, and the debate between חזקיה and רבי יוחנן over היזק שאינו ניכר
overview: The amud opens with two Sages arguing over whether the משנה lists מדמע (mixing תרומה into someone's food). One says it is the same as מטמא (making food impure), so there is no need to list it. The other says the payment is a קנס, and one קנס cannot be learned from another. The גמרא then shows, with a צריכא, that each of the three cases (מטמא, מדמע, מנסך) teaches something new, and does the same for a ברייתא in which מדמע was added later. Next, חזקיה and רבי יוחנן argue about היזק שאינו ניכר, damage you cannot see. חזקיה says the Torah makes such a damager pay and חכמים exempted the שוגג so he would report. רבי יוחנן says the Torah exempts him and חכמים fined the מזיד to stop abuse. Two sources, about כהנים who were מפגל and about work done with מי חטאת and the פרה אדומה, are brought against חזקיה, and both are answered. The amud ends as the גמרא begins quoting רבא about מי חטאת, and the quote continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Ending of the question: making food impure is the same as mixing in תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The end of the reason given by the Sage who does not list מדמע: in his view, מדמע is the same as מטמא, so there is no need to list it separately.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Making someone's food impure] is the same as mixing תרומה into his food.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the גמרא in the middle of explaining a dispute about whether מדמע belongs in the list. This line finishes the reason of the Sage who leaves it out: מדמע is no different from מטמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases the food is mixed with or turned into something forbidden, so it can no longer be used normally. For this Sage, the two cases are the same, so listing מטמא already covers מדמע. Step 2 gives the other Sage's reason for listing מדמע anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: That is the same as; no different from
One who mixes תרומה into another person's חולין, so the whole mixture becomes forbidden to non-כהנים
One who makes another person's food ritually impure

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the end of one Sage's reason. The beginning of the sentence (that מטמא is the same as this) came just before this amud.

phrases.english: is the same as 'one who mixes in תרומה.'
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence that started earlier: 'one who makes food impure' is the same as this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the reason, begun before this amud, of the Sage who does not list מדמע.

steps.title: The other opinion: it is a penalty, and penalties are not learned from each other
steps.stepSummary: The other opinion has no problem. It holds that the payment is a קנס, and one קנס cannot be learned from another, so every case must be stated.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other opinion holds it is a penalty, and we do not learn one penalty from another penalty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the other opinion has no problem with the משנה listing every case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this view the payment is a קנס set by the רבנן, and a fine applies only where the רבנן actually set it. It cannot be stretched to a similar case. That is why מנסך must be listed on its own, even though it is so similar to מדמע.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one; the other side of the argument
A fine or penalty set by the רבנן
We do not learn or derive

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rule 'we don't learn a קנס from a קנס,' which the next step questions.

phrases.english: And the other one: it is a penalty,
phrases.notes: 'The other one' is שמואל, the Sage who does include מדמע in the משנה's list.

phrases.english: and we do not learn from one penalty [to another].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason of the other Sage, who includes מדמע in the משנה even though it resembles מטמא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Fines cannot be learned from one another, so each case needs to be stated on its own.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The cases look like copies of each other, so one should be enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each fine stands alone, so the משנה must list each case.

steps.title: Question: if we do learn one penalty from another, why list all the cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the opinion that does learn one קנס from another: then why does the משנה list מטמא, מדמע and מנסך?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the one who learns a penalty from a penalty, why do I need all these cases?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes further. It asks about someone who holds that one קנס can be learned from another: for him, listing every case looks unnecessary again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 2 worked only because penalties can't be learned from each other. If someone holds that they can, the משנה could have stated one case and we would learn the others. So the question about extra cases comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who learns or derives
Why do I need all these? A standard question about seemingly extra cases

phrases.english: And according to the one who learns a penalty from a penalty,
why do I need all these?
phrases.notes: 'All these' means the cases in the משנה: making food impure, mixing in תרומה, and pouring wine for idol worship.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דְּיָלֵיף קְנָסָא מִקְּנָסָא כֹּל הָנֵי לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the answer from step 2 and asks about the opinion that rejects its rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's listing of several penalty cases, according to the one who learns a קנס from a קנס
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If penalties can be learned from each other, one case would be enough, so the others look extra.

steps.title: Each case is needed: making food impure has special reasons that mixing does not
steps.stepSummary: צריכא: had the משנה taught only מטמא, we might think the fine comes from a reason special to that case, either total loss of תרומה or the ban on causing impurity to חולין in ארץ ישראל. Then we would not apply it to מדמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is necessary. For if it had taught only 'one who makes food impure': if it is תרומה, I would have said [he is fined] because he ruins it completely; and if he makes חולין impure, [he is fined] because it is forbidden to cause impurity to חולין in ארץ ישראל. But one who mixes in תרומה, I might say no [fine].
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that every case is needed. It begins by showing that from מטמא alone we could not have learned מדמע. Steps 5 and 6 finish this answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making food impure has two possible special reasons for a fine. Impure תרומה can't be eaten by anyone, so it is a total loss. Making חולין impure breaks the rule against causing impurity to חולין in ארץ ישראל. Mixing in תרומה has neither reason, since the mixture can still be sold to a כהן, so we might have thought there is no fine.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary; each case teaches something the others can't
I would have said; the mistaken first thought
He ruins it completely
Regular food that is not holy
To cause impurity

steps.whatToRemember: צריכא here means each penalty case has its own reason. מטמא has extra reasons (total loss of תרומה, or causing impurity in ארץ ישראל) that מדמע lacks, so מדמע had to be taught separately.
steps.confusionAlert: This answer is only for the opinion that does learn a קנס from a קנס. Even that opinion can't learn one case from another when the first case has a special reason the second lacks.

phrases.english: It is necessary; for if it had taught [only] 'one who makes impure':
if it is תרומה, I would have said [he is fined]
because he ruins it completely,
and if he makes חולין impure,
[he is fined] because it is forbidden to cause impurity
to חולין that are in ארץ ישראל;
but one who mixes in תרומה, I might say [he is] not [fined].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3 by showing that each case is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכא: each case has its own reasoning, so one can't be learned from another.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From מטמא alone I would have said the fine is because of total loss or because of causing impurity in ארץ ישראל, so מדמע would not be fined.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה had to teach מדמע on its own (the reasons for the other cases come next).

steps.title: Mixing alone would not teach the case of making food impure
steps.stepSummary: Continuing the צריכא: if the משנה had taught only מדמע, we might say the fine applies because mixing is common, but not to מטמא, which is uncommon.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the משנה had taught us only מדמע, we would say he is fined because it happens often. But one who makes food impure, which does not happen often, we would say is not fined.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps answering why every case is needed. It shows that the מדמע case by itself would not be enough to teach us the מטמא case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חכמים usually put fines on things that happen often. Mixing תרומה into someone's food is common, so a fine there makes sense. Making food impure is rare, so without being told, we would think no fine was set for it.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it had taught us (only this case)
Common, happens often
Which is uncommon
I would say no (the rule does not apply)

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only the one who mixes,
we would say he is fined because it is common,
but one who makes it impure, which is uncommon,
I would say: no fine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second part of the צריכא that began in step 4
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכא: each case teaches something the other cannot
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From מדמע alone, we might think the fine only applies to common damage.
steps.terutzMaskana: מטמא must be stated separately, since it is uncommon.

steps.title: Even the idol-wine pourer pays the fine, following רבי ירמיה
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה had taught only מטמא and מדמע, we would not apply the fine to מנסך, since he also faces a heavier punishment. The משנה teaches that he pays anyway, following רבי ירמיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the משנה had taught us מטמא and מדמע, we would say they are fined because no heavier punishment pushes the fine aside. But the מנסך does face a heavier punishment, so we would say he is not fined. The משנה teaches us that he is fined, as רבי ירמיה explained.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the last part of the צריכא. It explains why the מנסך case also had to be written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule that when one act brings two punishments, a person gets only the heavier one (קים ליה בדרבה מיניה). The מנסך worships an idol, which carries a death penalty, so we might think that swallows up the money fine. רבי ירמיה explained that he becomes liable for the wine when he first lifts it, before the idol worship happens, so the fine still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: He receives the greater punishment (only the heavier punishment is given for one act)
One who pours someone else's wine as an offering to an idol
It comes to teach us

steps.whatToRemember: All three cases are needed. מטמא and מדמע each have their own special feature, and מנסך teaches that a heavier punishment does not cancel the fine, because of רבי ירמיה's explanation.
steps.whyThisMatters: This finishes the defense of the opinion that one fine can be learned from another. Even under that view, every case in the משנה adds something new.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us the one who makes impure and the one who mixes,

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא קִים לֵיהּ בִּדְרַבָּה מִינֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: we would say they are fined because there he does not receive a greater punishment,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מְנַסֵּךְ, דְּקִים לֵיהּ בִּדְרַבָּה מִינֵּיהּ –
phrases.english: but the one who pours the wine to an idol, where he does receive the greater punishment,
I would say: no fine.
So it teaches us that he is fined, as רבי ירמיה said.
phrases.notes: This points back to רבי ירמיה's earlier teaching: lifting the wine already makes it his, so he owes the fine before the idol worship happens.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third and final part of the צריכא, completing the answer to step 3
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכא, backed up by an outside explanation (רבי ירמיה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The death penalty for idol worship would cancel the fine for the מנסך.
steps.terutzMaskana: The מנסך is fined, because he owes the wine from the moment he lifts it, before the death-penalty act.

steps.title: In the version where mixing was added later, why was it needed?
steps.stepSummary: According to the ברייתא of אבוה דרבי אבין, at first only מטמא and מנסך were fined, and later מדמע was added. Why were all of these needed?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to what the father of רבי אבין taught: at first they said the one who makes impure and the one who pours to an idol are fined, and later they said that even the one who mixes is fined. Why do I need all of these?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge, based on a different version of the law. In that version, מדמע was only added later, and the גמרא asks why it was needed at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the view that one fine can be learned from another, once מטמא and מנסך were both fined, מדמע should follow on its own. Why did חכמים need to come back and add it?

keyTerms.meaning: The father of רבי אבין, who taught this ברייתא
At first, originally
They later changed and said
Why do I need all of these?

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the same question as step 3. Here the order matters: מדמע was added after מטמא and מנסך were already known, so the question is why that later addition was needed.

phrases.english: And according to what the father of רבי אבין taught:
At first they would say
the one who makes impure and the one who pours to an idol are fined,
then they came back and said: even the one who mixes,
why do I need all these?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the צריכא just completed to raise a new difficulty from a different version of the ruling
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא of אבוה דרבי אבין, read with the opinion that one fine can be learned from another
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: מדמע is common and has no heavier punishment, so it should follow from מטמא and מנסך. Adding it later seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Why מטמא alone would not teach us מנסך
steps.stepSummary: If only מטמא were taught, we might think the fine applies there because there is no bigger punishment involved. With מנסך, idolatry brings a bigger punishment, so we might think he does not pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: All three cases are needed. If we were taught only about one who makes food impure, we might say he pays because he gets no greater punishment. But one who pours wine for idolatry does face a greater punishment, so I would say he does not pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins answering the question of step 7 with a צריכא, starting with why מטמא alone would not be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule that someone who earns a death penalty for an act does not also pay money for it (קים ליה בדרבה מיניה). מטמא has no death penalty, so a fine there is easy. Pouring wine for idolatry is a capital act, so without the explicit teaching we might exempt him from paying.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary: each case teaches something new
He receives the greater punishment, so he does not also pay money
One who makes someone else's food impure
One who pours someone else's wine as an offering to idols
I would say not (the law would not apply)

steps.confusionAlert: This צריכא answers the ברייתא of אבוה דרבי אבין from step 7, not the משנה's list from steps 4-6. That is why the reasons here differ from the earlier צריכא.

phrases.english: It is necessary;
for if it had taught us only one who makes impure,

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא קִים לֵיהּ בִּדְרַבָּה מִינֵּיהּ;
phrases.english: [he pays] because he does not receive a greater punishment;
but one who pours [wine for idolatry],
who does receive the greater punishment,
I would say [he does] not [pay];

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering step 7's question of why the ברייתא lists all the cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From מטמא alone we would not fine the מנסך, since he faces a greater punishment.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא lists מנסך to teach that he pays even so.

steps.title: Why מנסך alone would not teach us מטמא
steps.stepSummary: If only מנסך were taught, we might think the fine applies because the wine is ruined completely. Impure food is not completely ruined, so we might not fine the מטמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if we were taught only about one who pours wine for idolatry, we might say he pays because he ruins it completely. But one who makes food impure does not ruin it completely, so I would say he does not pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the צריכא in the other direction: why מנסך alone would not be enough to teach מטמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wine poured for idolatry becomes totally forbidden, so the loss is complete. Impure food still has some use, so the loss is only partial. That difference might have made us think only the total-loss case gets fined.

keyTerms.meaning: It taught us
He ruins it completely

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only one who pours,
[he pays] because he ruins it completely;
but one who makes impure,
who does not ruin it completely,
I would say [he does] not [pay];

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second part of the same צריכא, reversing the direction.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From מנסך alone we would think only total loss is fined, not מטמא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא lists מטמא to teach that partial loss is fined too.

steps.title: Why the first two would not teach us מדמע
steps.stepSummary: Both מטמא and מנסך cause a big loss. מדמע causes only a small loss, so we might not fine him. That is why all three are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if we were taught only these two, we might say they pay because the loss is large. But one who mixes in תרומה causes only a small loss, so I would say he does not pay. Therefore all are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the צריכא by explaining why מדמע had to be added, and concludes that every case is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even together, מטמא and מנסך share a big loss. מדמע only lowers the value of the produce without destroying it, so we might have thought a small loss is not fined. This matches the ברייתא's history of adding מדמע later.

keyTerms.meaning: One who mixes תרומה into someone else's ordinary produce
A large loss
A small loss

steps.whatToRemember: Each of the three fined cases teaches its own point: a fine applies even with a greater punishment (מנסך), even with partial loss (מטמא), and even with small loss (מדמע).

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only these two,
[they pay] because the loss is large;
but one who mixes in תרומה,
where the loss is small,
I would say [he does] not [pay];
[so all are] necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the צריכא and closes the question of step 7.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the two big-loss cases we would not fine the מדמע, whose loss is small.
steps.terutzMaskana: מדמע is fined too, so all three cases are needed.

steps.title: חזקיה: by Torah law, accidental and deliberate are both liable
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה rules that by Torah law, whether the damage was done accidentally or on purpose, the person is liable to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said: By Torah law, whether accidental or deliberate, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: the משנה's rule that an accidental damager is exempt. חזקיה states that by Torah law even the accidental one is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה exempts the שוגג, but חזקיה says the Torah itself makes both שוגג and מזיד liable. That means the exemption for שוגג is not Torah law. The גמרא will next ask for his reason.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law
One who acts accidentally
One who acts deliberately
Liable (must pay)

phrases.english: חזקיה said:
By Torah law,
whether accidental or deliberate,
he is liable.
phrases.notes: This refers to the damages in our משנה, like making someone's food impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic on the משנה's שוגג/מזיד distinction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law, one who causes these damages is liable whether he acted accidentally or deliberately.

steps.title: The reason: hidden damage still counts as damage
steps.stepSummary: The reason for חזקיה's ruling is that damage you cannot see is still considered damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Damage that cannot be seen is still called damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind חזקיה's ruling and answers it right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When food becomes impure or wine becomes forbidden, it looks exactly the same, yet its value drops. חזקיה holds that this hidden damage (היזק שאינו ניכר) counts as real damage, so the Torah makes the damager pay like any other damager.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?
Damage that cannot be seen
Is considered damage

steps.whyThisMatters: היזק שאינו ניכר is a key idea: it decides whether changing an item's halachic status, without touching it physically, counts as damaging it.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Damage that cannot be seen is called damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for חזקיה's ruling in step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is even the accidental damager liable by Torah law?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because damage that cannot be seen still counts as damage.

steps.title: Why חכמים exempted the accidental damager
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה explains that the Sages exempted the שוגג so that he will tell the owner about the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did חכמים say that if he did it by accident he is exempt? So that he will tell the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues חזקיה's view. If by Torah law even the שוגג must pay, why did the Sages exempt him? The answer: so that he will tell the owner what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hidden damage cannot be seen, so the owner might eat impure food or use forbidden wine without knowing. If the שוגג had to pay, he might keep quiet to save money. By exempting him, the Sages make sure he speaks up and the owner does not come to sin.

keyTerms.meaning: So that he will inform him (the owner)

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that, according to חזקיה, the exemption for the שוגג in the משנה is a rabbinic rule laid on top of a Torah obligation to pay.

phrases.english: And what is the reason they said
phrases.notes: "They" means the Sages. By Torah law חזקיה holds he must pay, so this exemption comes from the Sages.

phrases.english: that if he did it unintentionally he is exempt?
So that he will inform him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how חזקיה fits the משנה's exemption for the שוגג with his ruling that the Torah makes him liable.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The Sages exempted the שוגג so that he will not hide the damage, and will tell the owner.

steps.title: Then the intentional damager should be exempt too
steps.stepSummary: If the goal is to get the damager to tell the owner, the מזיד should also be exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, he should be exempt even if he did it on purpose!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason just given. The same worry about keeping quiet should apply to someone who did the damage on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If exempting the damager is what gets him to report, then the מזיד should also be exempt, so he too will tell. But the משנה makes the מזיד pay, so the reason seems not to fit.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
Even when done on purpose as well

phrases.english: If so,
even if he did it intentionally as well he should be exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in step 13 by applying it to the מזיד.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that the שוגג is exempt so that he will inform the owner
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reason applies equally to the מזיד, yet the משנה makes the מזיד liable.

steps.title: Someone who wants to hurt will surely tell
steps.stepSummary: A person who damages on purpose wants the owner to know, so there is no need to exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, if he is trying to cause damage, would he not tell him?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Someone who did the damage on purpose will definitely tell the owner, so there is no need to exempt him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole point of damaging on purpose is to hurt the owner. If the owner never finds out, he suffers no loss, because he would just eat the food. So the מזיד will surely announce what he did, and the Sages had no reason to exempt him.

keyTerms.meaning: Now (meaning: seeing that...)
To cause damage
He intends
To inform

steps.whatToRemember: According to חזקיה, the Torah makes both the שוגג and the מזיד pay. The Sages exempted only the שוגג, so that he would report. The מזיד will report anyway, so he still pays.

phrases.english: Now, since he intends to cause damage,
will he not inform him?!
phrases.notes: If the owner never finds out, he loses nothing. So someone trying to cause harm will make sure the owner knows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 14 by showing the worry does not apply to the מזיד.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by the damager's motive
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Exempting the damager is needed to get him to report, so the מזיד should be exempt too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The מזיד wants the owner to know about the damage, so he will report even if he has to pay.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: by Torah law both are exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן argues with חזקיה and holds that by Torah law neither the שוגג nor the מזיד pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: By Torah law, whether he did it by accident or on purpose, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new opinion comes in. רבי יוחנן says that by Torah law, the person who caused the hidden damage does not have to pay at all, whether or not he meant to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the exact opposite of חזקיה, who said both are liable by Torah law. For רבי יוחנן, any payment in the משנה must therefore come from the Sages, not from the Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law
Whether accidental or intentional
Exempt (from paying)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two opinions. חזקיה says the Torah makes both pay. רבי יוחנן says the Torah makes both exempt.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
By Torah law,
whether unintentional or intentional,
he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents the opinion opposing חזקיה's ruling from step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law, one who causes hidden damage is exempt, whether he acted accidentally or on purpose.

steps.title: Hidden damage is not counted as damage
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's reason: damage that cannot be seen is not legally considered damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Damage that cannot be seen is not called damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason for רבי יוחנן's ruling: damage you cannot see is not considered damage at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The food or wine looks exactly the same as before. Since nothing physical changed, the Torah does not count it as damage, so there is nothing to pay for. This is the exact opposite of חזקיה's reason in step 12.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage that is not visible
Is not called damage

steps.whyThisMatters: The whole argument comes down to one question: does hidden damage count as damage or not?

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Damage that is not evident
is not called damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר לָא שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind רבי יוחנן's ruling in step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Hidden damage is not legally considered damage.

steps.title: Why חכמים fined the intentional damager
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the Sages made the מזיד pay so that people would not ruin others' food and claim they are exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did חכמים say that one who did it on purpose is liable? So that people would not go around making their friends' pure food impure and saying, "I am exempt."
steps.whatsHappening: If the Torah exempts everyone, why does the משנה make the מזיד pay? רבי יוחנן answers that the Sages added a fine so that people would not damage others on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without a fine, anyone could ruin his neighbor's food or wine on purpose and walk away free. The Sages fined only the מזיד to stop this abuse. The שוגג did not do it deliberately, so no fine was needed for him.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable (must pay)
His pure foods
His fellow
I am exempt

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, the Torah exempts both. The Sages fined only the מזיד, so that people would not damage others on purpose. This is the opposite structure from חזקיה.

phrases.english: And what is the reason they said
that if he did it intentionally he is liable?
So that it will not be that each and every person
goes and makes his fellow's pure foods impure,
and says, "I am exempt."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fits the משנה's liability for the מזיד into רבי יוחנן's Torah-law exemption.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The Sages fined the מזיד so that people would not deliberately damage others while claiming they are exempt.

steps.title: The case of כהנים who were מפגל on purpose
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: כהנים who were מפגל an offering on purpose must pay, and a ברייתא adds this is מפני תיקון העולם. This sets up a challenge.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה: כהנים who were מפגל an offering in the מקדש on purpose are liable. And a ברייתא taught about this: it is because of תיקון העולם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is bringing a source to set up a challenge. The משנה says that כהנים who ruin an offering through פיגול on purpose must pay, and a ברייתא says this rule is מפני תיקון העולם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פיגול is also damage you cannot see, because the offering looks the same. Calling the payment מפני תיקון העולם suggests it is a rabbinic fine, meaning that without it they would be exempt. That seems to fit רבי יוחנן and to clash with חזקיה, who says the Torah already makes them pay. The challenge itself is spelled out next.

keyTerms.meaning: They made an offering פיגול with a forbidden thought during the service
And a ברייתא taught about it
Improving society, a rule set up by the Sages

phrases.english: We learned: Priests who made an offering piggul in the Temple,
phrases.notes: פיגול means thinking, during the service, of eating or offering it after its proper time. That thought ruins the offering, even though it looks the same.

phrases.english: if they did so intentionally, they are liable;
and it was taught about it:
because of the betterment of the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both opinions are laid out, the גמרא brings a משנה to test them, aimed first at חזקיה.
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's ruling that by Torah law hidden damage must be paid for
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the Torah already makes the damager pay, the ברייתא would not need to call the payment for פיגול a rule of תיקון העולם.

steps.title: If unseen damage counts, the ברייתא should say the reason for exempting the שוגג
steps.stepSummary: According to חזקיה, a מזיד who was מפגל already pays by Torah law. So the reason 'מפני תיקון העולם' should explain why the שוגג is exempt, not why the מזיד pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that damage you cannot see is still called damage, then the ברייתא should have said: 'Those who did it by accident are exempt, because of תיקון העולם.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges חזקיה using the ברייתא from the previous step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חזקיה holds that unseen damage counts as damage by Torah law. Then a כהן who was מפגל on purpose already has to pay by Torah law, so no rabbinic reason is needed to make him pay. The ברייתא's reason 'תיקון העולם' only makes sense if it explains something רבנן added, like exempting the שוגג.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (introduces the opinion being tested)
Those who did it by accident
It should have said
Fixing society; a rule the Rabbis made for the public good

phrases.english: And if you say
that damage which cannot be seen is called damage,
then this should be: 'Unintentional ones are exempt'
'because of the betterment of the world.' That is what it should have said!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the משנה and ברייתא quoted in step 19 to challenge חזקיה.
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's view that unseen damage counts as damage by Torah law.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the מזיד already pays by Torah law, the rabbinic reason 'תיקון העולם' cannot be explaining why he pays. It should be explaining an exemption for the שוגג.

steps.title: The ברייתא really means the שוגג is exempt because of תיקון העולם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the ברייתא differently: the מזיד is liable, and the שוגג is exempt because of תיקון העולם.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is indeed what it is saying: those who did it on purpose are liable, but those who did it by accident are exempt, because of תיקון העולם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא's words can be read exactly the way the question wanted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason 'מפני תיקון העולם' is moved over to the second half of the case. The מזיד pays by Torah law, as חזקיה holds. The שוגג would also owe by Torah law, but רבנן exempted him for the good of society. So the ברייתא fits חזקיה after all.

keyTerms.meaning: That is indeed what it is saying
But (this implies)

phrases.english: That is indeed what it is saying:
Those who did it on purpose are liable;
but those who did it by accident are exempt
because of the betterment of the world.

steps.confusionAlert: The words of the ברייתא do not change. Only how we read them changes: 'תיקון העולם' now explains the exemption of the שוגג, not the payment of the מזיד.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20 by agreeing with its reading.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the source (the reason belongs to the second half)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought 'תיקון העולם' was the reason the מזיד pays.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'תיקון העולם' is the reason the שוגג is exempt, so the ברייתא fits חזקיה.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר challenges from work done with מי חטאת and פרה אדומה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that someone who does work with מי חטאת or the פרה אדומה is exempt in a human court. If unseen damage counts, he should be liable there too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר challenged: someone who does work with the purification water or the red heifer is exempt by human law but liable by the laws of Heaven. If unseen damage counts as damage, he should be liable by human law too!
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge to חזקיה, this time from a ברייתא about the פרה אדומה and its water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doing work with the פרה אדומה or with מי חטאת makes them unfit, but you cannot see any change in them. That is exactly היזק שאינו ניכר. The ברייתא exempts him in a human court, which fits רבי יוחנן and seems to go against חזקיה.

keyTerms.meaning: Purification water, mixed with the ashes of the פרה אדומה
The red heifer (פרה אדומה)
Human courts, where payment can be forced
The laws of Heaven, a duty between him and ה׳

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar raised an objection:
One who does work with the purification water
or with the red heifer,
is exempt by human law
but liable by the laws of Heaven.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ הֶיזֵּק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִיכָּר שְׁמֵיהּ הֶיזֵּק,
phrases.english: And if you say that damage which cannot be seen is called damage,
then he should be liable by human law too!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first challenge was answered, a fresh challenge to חזקיה comes from a different ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's view that unseen damage counts as damage by Torah law.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Making the פרה or the water unfit is unseen damage. Yet the ברייתא exempts him in a human court, which matches רבי יוחנן and not חזקיה.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר answers himself: the cases involve very indirect actions
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains the ברייתא as talking about unusual cases. In each one, the person did not directly use them for work, so even חזקיה agrees he is exempt in a human court.
steps.simpleTranslation: He raised the question and he answered it. The heifer: he put it into the calf pen so that it would nurse and also thresh. The purification water: he weighed weights against it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers his own question by limiting the ברייתא to special cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the heifer, the person only brought it in to nurse, and the threshing happened along the way. With the water, he only used it as a counterweight on a scale. These are not normal acts of putting them to work, so being exempt in a human court does not prove that unseen damage is not damage. חזקיה's view stands.

keyTerms.term: הוּא מוֹתֵיב לַהּ וְהוּא מְפָרֵק לַהּ
keyTerms.meaning: He raised the question and he answered it himself
A pen or stall for calves
It would thresh (tread on grain)
Weights for a scale

steps.whatToRemember: Both challenges to חזקיה are answered. The ברייתא about מפגל can be re-read to fit him. The case of מי חטאת and the פרה is limited to very indirect actions, so it does not prove that unseen damage is not damage.

phrases.aramaic: הוּא מוֹתֵיב לַהּ – וְהוּא מְפָרֵק לַהּ:
phrases.english: He raised the objection, and he himself resolved it:
The heifer: he brought it into the calf pen
so that it would nurse and also thresh;
The purification water: he weighed weights against it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא מוֹתֵיב לַהּ וְהוּא מְפָרֵק לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי אלעזר's challenge from step 22 by narrowing the ברייתא's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא talks about any work done with the פרה or the water, so his exemption seems to show that unseen damage is not damage.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is talking only about very indirect actions, which are exempt in a human court for that reason. חזקיה's view is not disproven.

steps.title: The גמרא begins quoting רבא about the water of purification
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a challenge with 'והאמר רבא' and starts quoting רבא's statement about מי חטאת.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבא say: water of purification...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It starts a challenge by quoting רבא, and the quote continues in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'והאמר' means 'but didn't he say?' It signals that a statement from רבא is about to clash with something just said. The גמרא brings it right after רבי אלעזר's explanation of the מי חטאת cases, so the full quote will show what the problem is.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? This is a standard opening for a challenge.

steps.confusionAlert: This is only the opening of רבא's statement. Don't try to work out the challenge yet; the actual ruling comes in the next lines.

phrases.english: But didn't Rava say:
Water of purification
phrases.notes: This is the water mixed with the ashes of the פרה אדומה from Step 22. רבא's sentence continues in the next lines.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge against רבי אלעזר's explanation of the ברייתא about מי חטאת in Step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's explanation of the ברייתא about מי חטאת in Step 23.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The גמרא introduces a statement of רבא about מי חטאת that seems to conflict with what was just said. The full point of conflict is spelled out in the continuation of the quote.
